deepDive.title: Thermal expansion — why railway tracks have gaps and bridges have rollers
deepDive.body: In Class 7 you saw thermometers use thermal expansion of mercury. Class 8 quantifies the same effect for solids. Every solid has a LINEAR EXPANSION COEFFICIENT — how much its length grows per °C of warming. Steel: 12 × 10⁻⁶ per °C. So a 100-metre steel railway track at 20°C, on a 45°C summer day, grows by 100 × 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 25 = 0.030 m = 3 cm. Without expansion gaps, the track would BUCKLE — bend sideways in deadly waves. Indian Railways inserts ~20 mm gaps every 30 m for exactly this reason. The Howrah Bridge in Kolkata sits on giant ROLLERS that let it slide a few cm in summer (and back in winter). Engineers don't fight expansion; they design for it.
deepDive.nextStepHint: Class 11 derives ΔL = αLΔT and uses it for bimetallic strips in thermostats.

deepDive.title: Specific heat capacity — why water saves your city from the heat
deepDive.body: In Class 7 you saw water has special properties. Class 10 names the property: SPECIFIC HEAT CAPACITY — how much energy (joules) it takes to raise 1 kg by 1°C. Water's value: 4186 J/kg/°C. Sand's: ~830. So water heats up 5× SLOWER than sand for the same energy input. This is why Mumbai (surrounded by Arabian Sea) has milder summers than Delhi (inland) — even though both at same latitude. The sea acts as a giant thermal buffer. Same physics in reverse during winter: the sea stays warm longer, so coastal Goa is milder than inland Madhya Pradesh. Indian coastal cities thank water's specific heat for ~10°C less extreme weather than their inland counterparts.
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle after heat vs temperature basics.
deepDive.nextStepHint: JEE / Class 11 introduces calorimetry — measuring specific heat experimentally.

deepDive.title: Kinetic theory of gases — heat is just movement
deepDive.body: Class 7 said heat is the energy of warm things. Class 11 reveals what HEAT actually is at atomic scale: heat is the average KINETIC ENERGY (motion energy) of the atoms or molecules. A hot gas = molecules bouncing fast (~500 m/s at room temperature for air). Cold gas = molecules bouncing slowly. Temperature is proportional to this average speed squared: T ∝ v². When you touch a hot stove, fast-moving stove atoms collide with your skin's atoms, transferring kinetic energy. There's no 'heat substance' — just motion. Indian physicist S.N. Bose's 1924 work was about gases of indistinguishable particles — that's how he and Einstein found the Bose-Einstein statistics. The whole field of statistical mechanics traces back to this insight: heat = motion.
deepDive.nextStepHint: Class 12 covers Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution — the curve of molecular speeds at a given temperature.
